title: Les éléments chauffants Tempora & Elhami (QC Court)
subject: Court of Quebec criminal prosecution of a corporation and its principals for fraudulent SR&ED tax credit claims.
outcome: Accused convicted of tax fraud and fined for filing false and fabricated SR&ED claims.
summary: Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. and its directors, Maged and Shady Elhami, were convicted by the Court of Quebec (2017 QCCQ 2684) for claiming $1,324,294 in unwarranted SR&ED investment tax credits using backdated invoices. The key takeaway for Canadian claimants: fines apply to the credit claimed, even when the CRA pays nothing out.
metaDescription: Review the Court of Quebec decision involving Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc, Maged Elhami, and Shady Elhami on tax claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Overview of the Taxpayer's Claim and Corporate Profile

The multi-forum litigation surrounding Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. (Tempora Heating Elements Inc., hereinafter "Tempora") and its directors and shareholders, Maged Elhami and Shady Elhami, constitutes one of the most consequential enforcement landmarks in the history of the Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) (Recherche scientifique et développement expérimental — RS&DE) tax incentive program. Operating from facilities at 2501 Dollard Avenue in the Borough of LaSalle, Montréal, Province of Quebec, Tempora functioned as an industrial manufacturer specializing in electric heating elements, thermal components, railway track heating platforms, and commercial drying equipment. Across the 2006 through 2010 taxation years, Tempora systematically utilized the federal SR&ED regime under the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (Loi de l'impôt sur le revenu — L.I.R.) to claim refundable Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) (Crédits d'impôt à l'investissement — CII).

The dispute between Tempora and the Crown evolved across two distinct but factually intertwined judicial tracks in Canada: a landmark criminal prosecution adjudicated by the Court of Quebec, Criminal and Penal Chamber (Cour du Québec, Chambre criminelle et pénale, Docket No. 500-73-004048-134, 2017 QCCQ 2684) regarding Tempora's 2010 taxation year, and a companion civil reassessment appeal adjudicated by the Tax Court of Canada (Cour canadienne de l'impôt, 2025 TCC 173) regarding Tempora's 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2009 taxation years. Taken together, these two decisions establish the definitive modern boundary between legitimate technical claiming, negligent misrepresentation that reopens statute-barred taxation years, and criminal tax fraud in the Canadian SR&ED sphere.

In the penal proceeding at the heart of 2017 QCCQ 2684, Tempora and its two principals filed a 2010 SR&ED claim seeking $1,324,294 in federal Investment Tax Credits. Because Tempora's principals sought, as the Court found, to make a quick and easy financial gain (gain financier rapide et facile), Maged Elhami and Shady Elhami fabricated a massive third-party R&D expenditure claim anchored on two detailed, antedated (backdated) commercial invoices totalling more than $4,500,000 purportedly issued by an arm's-length engineering firm, Pyro Genesis (PyroGenesis). The defendants delivered these backdated invoices to their external accountant to record the nonexistent R&D expenditures in Tempora's corporate books and financial statements (états financiers), which were subsequently transmitted to the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) (Agence du revenu du Canada — ARC) alongside the prescribed SR&ED forms to claim the $1,324,294 credit. In reality, no contract had ever been confirmed between Tempora and Pyro Genesis, Pyro Genesis had never performed any of the alleged R&D work, Pyro Genesis did not know that its invoices were going to be used for fraudulent purposes, and Tempora was legally entitled to $0 of the $1,324,294 credit claimed.
The Tax Authority's Challenge and Audit Investigation

The CRA's intervention against Tempora illustrates the operational mechanics of Canada's dual civil-verification and criminal-investigation enforcement framework. When Tempora filed its 2010 SR&ED claim requesting $1,324,294 in refundable tax credits, the CRA placed the claim under pre-disbursement fiscal and technical control. During this initial verification stage, CRA audit officials requested supporting documentation to substantiate the $4,500,000+ third-party expenditure claim. Rather than withdrawing the unfounded claim, one of the Elhami brothers transmitted the two false Pyro Genesis invoices directly to the CRA. During a subsequent telephone conference with the CRA's Assistant Director of Audit, Maged Elhami explicitly lied to the tax authority by confirming that Pyro Genesis had executed the R&D work on Tempora's behalf.

As the CRA prepared for a planned visit to Tempora's premises, Shady Elhami contacted Pyro Genesis directly just prior to the scheduled CRA visit and attempted to persuade Pyro Genesis representatives to display industrial equipment to the visiting CRA officials and falsely confirm that the R&D project had been executed. Pyro Genesis refused to participate in the deception. Thereafter, on the morning of the CRA visit, Tempora amended its ITC application. The CRA refused the amendments and did not approve Tempora's file, so the defendants received no benefit from the offence; the matter then proceeded as a federal prosecution by way of summary conviction, conducted by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada (PPSC) (Service des poursuites pénales du Canada — SPPC), and the prosecution asked the Court to take into account the CRA's estimate of approximately $204,000 in costs for the tax audit the CRA had to conduct.

Separately, the CRA also conducted an exhaustive retrospective civil audit of Tempora's previously processed SR&ED claims for the 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2009 taxation years, including years that the CRA had initially processed on an "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) basis. During that civil audit, CRA reviewers discovered that Tempora's technical narratives contained background theory and technical text plagiarized directly from third-party supplier and manufacturer websites. On that basis, the Minister of National Revenue reopened the statute-barred taxation years under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA, disallowed the 2006 and 2009 SR&ED claims in full and the 2007 and 2008 claims in part, imposed gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA, and pursued derivative shareholder liability assessments under section 160 ITA.
Governing Canadian Statutory Framework

The judicial adjudication of Tempora's SR&ED claims operates across three intersecting statutory pillars of the federal Income Tax Act (Loi de l'impôt sur le revenu) and the Criminal Code (Code criminel). The first pillar governs the criminal prosecution of fraudulent refund and credit claims under subsection 239(1.1) ITA (paragraphe 239(1.1) L.I.R.). Applicable to refundable tax credit programs such as the SR&ED ITC regime, paragraph 239(1.1)(a) ITA (alinéa 239(1.1)a) L.I.R.) makes it an offence for any person to make, or participate in, assent to, or acquiesce in the making of, false or misleading statements in a return, certificate, statement, or answer filed or made under the ITA in order to obtain or claim an unwarranted refund or credit. Complementing that provision, paragraph 239(1.1)(c) ITA (alinéa 239(1.1)c) L.I.R.) criminalizes making, or assenting to or acquiescing in the making of, false or deceptive entries in corporate books or records to obtain or claim an unwarranted credit. Under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA (alinéa 239(1.1)g) L.I.R.), an offender convicted on summary conviction faces a mandatory statutory fine between 50% and 200% of the amount by which the refund or credit obtained or claimed exceeds the amount to which the person is entitled (or, under paragraph 239(1.1)(h) ITA, both that fine and imprisonment for up to two years); the Court of Quebec read this single paragraph as covering three distinct cases (cas de figure): (a) the excess refund, (b) the excess credit obtained, and (c) the excess credit claimed (crédit demandé) over the amount to which the person is entitled. Sentencing within this statutory range is further governed by the fundamental objectives of denunciation, general and specific deterrence, and proportionality codified in sections 718 to 718.2 of the Criminal Code.

The second statutory pillar governs substantive SR&ED eligibility and expenditure qualification under subsection 248(1), section 37, and section 127 ITA. To qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, the claimant must prove that its activities satisfy the strict statutory definition of scientific research and experimental development in subsection 248(1) ITA, which requires a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis for the advancement of scientific knowledge or the achievement of technological advancement. Once substantive eligibility is established, qualifying current expenditures—comprising direct SR&ED salaries and wages, materials consumed or transformed (matériaux consommés ou transformés), and eligible Canadian subcontractor payments—are pooled under section 37 ITA and earn Investment Tax Credits under subsections 127(5) and 127(9) ITA, claimed via prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31.

The third statutory pillar governs civil limitation periods, gross negligence penalties, and derivative shareholder liability under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i), subsection 163(2), and section 160 ITA. Where the CRA seeks to reassess an SR&ED claim after the expiration of the normal three- or four-year reassessment period, subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA empowers the Minister to reopen statute-barred taxation years if the taxpayer or person filing the return has made any misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default (présentation erronée des faits, par négligence, inattention ou omission volontaire), or has committed fraud. Where the misrepresentation involves a high degree of culpable conduct or reckless disregard for compliance, subsection 163(2) ITA imposes civil gross negligence penalties (pénalités pour faute lourde) equal to 50% of the overstated credit or understated tax. Finally, where a retroactive SR&ED reassessment leaves a corporation with unpaid tax debts, section 160 ITA imposes strict joint and several liability (responsabilité solidaire) on non-arm's-length transferees—including controlling shareholders who received dividends or corporate transfers during the reassessed years—up to the amount by which the fair market value of the property transferred exceeds the fair market value of any consideration given for it, without any statutory limitation period or due diligence defence.
The Court's Final Holding and Subsequent Procedural History

In the primary criminal proceeding before the Court of Quebec (2017 QCCQ 2684, Docket No. 500-73-004048-134), following seven days of trial and sentencing hearings across 2015 and 2016, the Honourable Judge Christian M. Tremblay, J.C.Q., convicted Maged Elhami, Shady Elhami, and Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. on October 17, 2016, on both Count 1 (paragraph 239(1.1)(a) ITA) and Count 2 (paragraph 239(1.1)(c) ITA). In the written sentencing judgment delivered on March 27, 2017, Judge Tremblay rejected the defence's contention that no statutory fine could be levied under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA because the CRA had blocked payment before any funds were disbursed. The Court held that paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA, which applies to a refund or credit "obtained or claimed", expressly targets the excess credit claimed ($1,324,294) regardless of whether any disbursement occurred. Emphasizing the careful planning and premeditation of the scheme, the defendants' attempt to lure CRA officials, and the joint participation of all three co-defendants in a common venture (aventure commune), and while finding that the situation could justify a fine above the 50% minimum, Judge Tremblay, accounting for the fact that both counts arose from the same transaction and for the totality of the fines, imposed the minimum statutory fine of 50% ($662,147) per count on each of the two counts against each of the three defendants, resulting in a fine of $1,324,294 per defendant and a combined global fine of $3,972,882, plus court costs and victim surcharges.

On summary conviction appeal, the Superior Court of Quebec (2018 QCCS 2576, March 22, 2018; reasons clarified May 9, 2018) allowed the appeal in part by upholding the convictions on Count 1, entering a conditional stay of proceedings (arrêt conditionnel des procédures) on Count 2 against multiple convictions for the same delict, and varying the fines to $1,000,000. The Court of Appeal of Quebec dismissed the defendants' subsequent motion for leave to appeal from the Superior Court judgment (Masse J.) on September 13, 2018 (2018 QCCA 1488), and the Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the application for leave to appeal on March 7, 2019 (Docket No. 38388). Subsequently, in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173, November 20, 2025), the Tax Court of Canada upheld the Minister's right to reopen the statute-barred 2006 through 2009 taxation years under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA due to plagiarized and negligent T661 documentation, denied the 2006 and 2009 SR&ED claims in full, sustained gross negligence penalties, and allowed only narrow portions of the 2007 and 2008 claims where Tempora produced physical evidence of consumables and documented test results.

body.text: 2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous legal and technical dissection of 2017 QCCQ 2684 and 2025 TCC 173 reveals six distinct evidentiary, contractual, technical, and accounting deficiencies that transformed Tempora's SR&ED claims into a combination of criminal convictions and decade-late civil reassessments.
Fabrication of Subcontractor Expenditures and Absence of Contractual Legal Obligation (Pyro Genesis)

In 2017 QCCQ 2684, the primary legal defect that invalidated the 2010 SR&ED claim and triggered criminal liability under paragraph 239(1.1)(a) ITA was the complete absence of a confirmed contract or actual performance of R&D work underlying the claimed third-party expenditures exceeding $4,500,000. Under the Canadian statutory regime governing subcontracted SR&ED—specifically subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) and subsection 127(9) ITA—a claimant may only include payments to an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor in its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool where an enforceable contractual obligation is incurred in the taxation year for SR&ED actually performed in Canada "on behalf of" (pour le compte de) the taxpayer. Furthermore, the underlying activities executed by the subcontractor must independently satisfy the technical criteria of subsection 248(1) ITA.

Tempora failed every requirement of this legal standard. Rather than entering into a definitive R&D subcontract with Pyro Genesis and tracking genuine experimental work during the 2010 fiscal period, Maged and Shady Elhami utilized two detailed, antedated (backdated) invoices from Pyro Genesis totalling more than $4,500,000 to manufacture a fictional expenditure base capable of generating $1,324,294 in refundable Investment Tax Credits. As Judge Tremblay emphasized in 2017 QCCQ 2684, no contract was ever confirmed between Tempora and Pyro Genesis, Pyro Genesis never performed the work described on those invoices, and Pyro Genesis did not know that the invoices were going to be used for fraudulent purposes. In Canadian tax law, unconfirmed commercial quotes, prospective budgetary estimates, or backdated invoices untethered to actual experimental execution during the fiscal year cannot create an incurred expenditure under section 37 ITA; when intentionally filed with the CRA to claim a tax credit, they establish the actus reus and mens rea of criminal tax fraud under paragraph 239(1.1)(a) ITA.
Falsification of Corporate Books and Instrumentalization of the External Accountant

A second decisive failure identified by the Court of Quebec in 2017 QCCQ 2684 was the deliberate corruption of Tempora's accounting books and financial statements (états financiers), which grounded the second count of conviction under paragraph 239(1.1)(c) ITA. Under Canadian SR&ED compliance procedures, the expenditures claimed on Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must reconcile directly to the corporate taxpayer's General Ledger (Grand livre) and General Index of Financial Information (Index général des renseignements financiers — IGRF / GIFI) submitted with the T2 corporate income tax return.

To fabricate this accounting reconciliation, the Elhami brothers delivered the two antedated Pyro Genesis invoices to Tempora's external accountant, intentionally deceiving the accountant into recording more than $4,500,000 in nonexistent R&D liabilities and preparing erroneous financial statements (états financiers erronés) that were then submitted to the CRA alongside the ITC claim. A critical second-order legal takeaway from 2017 QCCQ 2684 is how Canadian courts evaluate the involvement of external accounting or tax professionals when management supplies tainted source data. Rather than treating the accountant's involvement as any form of shield against penalties or mens rea, Judge Tremblay listed the fact that the Elhami brothers misled the accountant, who produced erroneous financial statements, as part of their careful planning and implementation of the fraudulent claim under the degree-of-premeditation factor (degré de préméditation) under the sentencing framework of Lévesque c. Procureur général du Québec, 1993 CanLII 4232 (QCCA).
Active Audit Obstruction, Subornation of Third-Party Witnesses, and the Inefficacy of Post-Detection Amendments

The Court of Quebec's decision in 2017 QCCQ 2684 also provides an authoritative warning regarding taxpayer conduct during a CRA pre-payment SR&ED review. When CRA officials initiated their audit verification of the 2010 claim and requested documentary support, the defendants engaged in a calculated sequence of obstructive acts rather than making a candid disclosure. First, one of the Elhami brothers transmitted the two false Pyro Genesis invoices directly to CRA auditors. Second, during a telephone conversation with the CRA's Assistant Audit Director, Maged Elhami affirmatively misrepresented the facts by confirming that Pyro Genesis had executed the R&D work. Third, immediately prior to the CRA's scheduled on-site inspection, Shady Elhami contacted Pyro Genesis and requested that the company display equipment to CRA officials and falsely corroborate that the R&D project had been performed. Fourth, only after Pyro Genesis refused to participate in the cover-up did Tempora submit an amended ITC application on the exact morning of the CRA site visit.

At sentencing, the defence advanced two subtle legal arguments designed to avoid the mandatory statutory fine under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA: first, that claiming SR&ED credits is less culpable than self-assessed income tax evasion because SR&ED applications undergo mandatory CRA pre-payout verification; and second, that because the CRA blocked the claim and disbursed $0 (the file never having been approved), no fine should be imposed under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA, since no refund or credit had been obtained. Judge Tremblay accepted that attempting to obtain ITCs, although a form of fraud, differs from evading tax under a self-assessment system, but rejected the argument that no fine could be imposed; in setting out the applicable sentencing principles, the Court relied on authorities including Knox Contracting Ltd. v. The Queen, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 338, R. v. McKinlay Transport Ltd., [1990] 1 S.C.R. 627, R. c. Coffin, 2006 QCCA 471, R. c. Avard, 2014 QCCQ 9716, and R. v. Global Enviro Inc. and McIntyre, 2011 ABQB 32 (in which, as the Court noted, the defendants were fined an amount equivalent to 77% of the ITC claim made to the CRA, or $250,000).

Drawing on R. c. Avard, Judge Tremblay noted that fraud against the government abuses the bond of public trust (lien de confiance) between the claimant and the state because tax authorities cannot systematically inspect every underlying transaction prior to processing. However, the Court found that, in this ITC context, the breach-of-trust factor was not entirely absent but was better described as an attempt to lure CRA officials, since the defendants tried to convince a third party (Pyro Genesis) to make false representations during the CRA's planned visit, rather than a full abuse of public trust (abus de confiance) of the kind that constitutes in itself an aggravating factor in self-assessment cases. Furthermore, as a matter of statutory interpretation, Judge Tremblay ruled that paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA does not confer three discretionary choices on the sentencing judge to waive fines when no refund is paid out; rather, the three cases it covers (the excess refund, the excess credit obtained and the excess credit claimed) address three distinct factual scenarios, with the third case mandating a fine of 50% to 200% of the excess credit claimed (crédit demandé) over actual entitlement. Because Tempora claimed an ITC of $1,324,294 when it was entitled to nothing, and the amendments it filed on the morning of the CRA visit were refused by the CRA, the Court applied the third case and calculated the fine on the $1,324,294 credit claimed, imposing the 50% minimum on each count.
Plagiarized Technical Narratives and Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty (2025 TCC 173)

While 2017 QCCQ 2684 addresses fabricated subcontractor invoices in the criminal sphere, the companion Tax Court of Canada judgment in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173) exposes the fatal technical and evidentiary defects that invalidated Tempora's earlier SR&ED claims for the 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2009 taxation years. Under subsection 248(1) ITA, the foundational threshold of any eligible SR&ED project is the existence of a genuine scientific or technological uncertainty (incertitude scientifique ou technologique)—meaning a technical system constraint or capability gap that cannot be resolved using standard engineering practice, publicly available scientific principles, or commercial vendor specifications.

In 2025 TCC 173, the CRA audit revealed that Tempora's Form T661 technical project narratives contained extensive background theory and technical descriptions plagiarized directly from third-party supplier and manufacturer websites. Before the Tax Court of Canada, Tempora argued that substantive entitlement to SR&ED tax credits depends on whether technological advancement occurred in the taxpayer's operations rather than on report formatting, and contended that copying background theory from vendor websites should not negate genuine shop-floor experimentation.

The Tax Court of Canada rejected Tempora's position and established two critical principles for Canadian R&D tax practitioners. First, on the substantive merits under subsection 248(1) ITA, relying on supplier or manufacturer websites as project evidence defeats the claimant's burden of proving technological uncertainty: vendor website material inherently reflects publicly available standard practice and commercial off-the-shelf engineering knowledge rather than a technological obstacle exceeding the current state of the art. Second, on the procedural threshold of subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA, presenting plagiarized third-party website content as authentic, project-specific SR&ED technical support renders the return misleading in context and constitutes a misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default. Consequently, even where the CRA had initially processed Tempora's SR&ED claims on an "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) basis years earlier, the negligent T661 narratives empowered the Minister to reopen the statute-barred 2006–2009 taxation years nearly a decade later and impose 50% gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA.
Lack of a Structured Process of Experimentation Versus Objective Physical Corroboration

The Tax Court's analysis in 2025 TCC 173 also provides a remarkably clear evidentiary contrast regarding how a taxpayer must prove a structured process of experimentation (processus d'expérimentation systématique) and contemporaneous documentation (documentation contemporaine). In Canadian SR&ED litigation, a company's subjective belief that it is innovating, or evidence that it developed a commercially successful product, is legally insufficient to qualify for SR&ED credits. Instead, the claimant must adduce objective, contemporaneous evidence demonstrating a scientific methodology: formulating testable hypotheses directed at resolving the technological uncertainty, executing systematic testing protocols, and recording measurable results.

Applying this strict evidentiary standard across the four reassessed years in 2025 TCC 173, the Tax Court reached a bifurcated outcome that underscores the decisive role of physical and contemporaneous shop-floor evidence. For the 2006 and 2009 taxation years, Tempora failed to produce objective evidence of formulated hypotheses, structured testing, or measurable experimental results; consequently, the Tax Court denied the 2006 and 2009 SR&ED claims in their entirety and upheld the gross negligence penalties. Conversely, for specific portions of projects carried out in the 2007 and 2008 taxation years, the Tax Court accepted Tempora's SR&ED eligibility specifically where Tempora produced objective physical evidence, consisting of documented consumables (matériaux consommés) and contemporaneously documented test results (résultats d'essais documentés). This divergence demonstrates that while plagiarized T661 narratives strip away the protection of the normal reassessment period under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA, objective physical artifacts—such as tracked material consumption and quantitative test logs generated during the year of experimentation—remain the sole evidentiary lifeline capable of substantiating SR&ED execution at trial.
Personal Culpability of Directors, Derivative Shareholder Liability Under Section 160 ITA, and Public Procurement Debarment

Finally, the Tempora jurisprudence illustrates how severe SR&ED compliance failures pierce the corporate veil to inflict personal financial and regulatory consequences on corporate directors and shareholders. In the criminal sphere (2017 QCCQ 2684), Judge Tremblay rejected any differentiation in culpability among Maged Elhami, Shady Elhami, and the corporate entity Tempora, holding that because the two brothers and their company acted in a common venture (aventure commune) to plan and execute the false claim, each of the three defendants bore equal responsibility and faced the identical statutory fine on each count. Moreover, defence counsel submitted at sentencing that, as a result of the conviction, Tempora would henceforth be inscribed on Quebec's Registre des entreprises non admissibles aux contrats publics (RENA), disqualifying the corporation from public-sector procurement contracts.

In the civil sphere (2025 TCC 173), reopening statute-barred SR&ED years a decade after initial processing creates an immediate personal hazard for owner-managers under section 160 ITA. When the Minister retroactively claws back four years of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits and adds compound daily arrears interest plus 50% gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA, the corporation suddenly owes a massive retroactive tax debt dating back to the reassessed years. Under section 160 ITA, any non-arm's-length transfer of property—such as dividends, shareholder draws, or unremunerated benefits—paid by the corporation to its shareholders during or after those reassessed years renders the recipient shareholders jointly and severally liable (solidairement responsables) for the corporation's underlying tax debt up to the amount transferred, with no due diligence defence available.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and judicial requirement examined across the Tempora litigation (2017 QCCQ 2684, 2018 QCCS 2576, 2018 QCCA 1488, and 2025 TCC 173) against the taxpayer's specific legal or evidentiary failures and the standard of proof enforced by Canadian courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure (Tempora Inc., Maged Elhami & Shady Elhami)
The Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: ITA s. 37(1)(a)(ii), s. 127(9) & s. 239(1.1)(a) (L.I.R. al. 37(1)a)(ii), par. 127(9) et al. 239(1.1)a))

Substantiation of Third-Party Subcontractor SR&ED Expenditures: Subcontracted R&D expenditures must be incurred pursuant to an enforceable contract for SR&ED actually performed in Canada on the taxpayer's behalf.
Submitted two backdated invoices totalling >$4,500,000 from Pyro Genesis to claim $1,324,294 in ITCs for 2010, despite having no confirmed contract and Pyro Genesis having performed no work.

Beyond a Reasonable Doubt (Criminal) / Balance of Probabilities (Civil): Taxpayer must produce an executed agreement, proof of actual R&D execution, and authentic billing. Filing fabricated third-party invoices constitutes criminal fraud under s. 239(1.1)(a) ITA.

Integrity of Books, Records, and Financial Statements: Accounting entries and GIFI financial statements supporting Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 must accurately reflect genuine, incurred transactions.
Delivered the fabricated Pyro Genesis invoices to the external accountant, misleading the accountant into recording false entries and preparing erroneous financial statements filed with the CRA.

Strict Documentary & Accounting Authenticity: Misleading the accountant with false source invoices, so that erroneous financial statements were produced, did not establish a "reliance on professional advice" defence (none was raised); instead, the Court considered it under the degree-of-premeditation factor (2017 QCCQ 2684, varied on Kienapple grounds in 2018 QCCS 2576).
ITA s. 239(1.1)(g) & Criminal Code ss. 718–718.2 (L.I.R. al. 239(1.1)g) et C.cr. art. 718–718.2)

Mandatory Fine on Unwarranted Credits Claimed & Pre-Verification Honesty: Statutory fine of 50% to 200% applies to the excess credit claimed, regardless of whether the CRA blocks disbursement prior to payout.

Maged Elhami lied to the CRA Assistant Audit Director; Shady Elhami asked Pyro Genesis to stage equipment and lie to CRA auditors; Tempora filed an amended claim on the morning of the site visit and argued $0 payout meant $0 fine.

Strict Statutory Application to Amount Claimed: The three cases covered by s. 239(1.1)(g) (excess refund, excess credit obtained, excess credit claimed) govern distinct factual scenarios, not judicial discretion to waive fines. The credit-claimed case applies to the $1,324,294 claimed. The Court accepted that an ITC claim subject to CRA verification differs from evasion under self-assessment, but found the breach-of-trust factor not entirely absent, as the defendants attempted to lure CRA officials (R. c. Coffin; R. c. Avard).
ITA s. 248(1) ("SR&ED") (L.I.R. par. 248(1) « RS&DE »)

Proof of Technological Uncertainty & Technological Advancement: The taxpayer must demonstrate an objective system-level or scientific uncertainty that cannot be resolved through standard practice or publicly available knowledge.
Copied theoretical background and technical descriptions directly from third-party supplier and manufacturer websites into Form T661 technical reports for 2006–2009 (2025 TCC 173).

Objective Technical Demarcation: Supplier and manufacturer website content represents publicly available standard knowledge, not technological uncertainty. Subjective belief in innovation or commercial success is legally insufficient (2025 TCC 173).
ITA s. 248(1) & s. 37(1) (L.I.R. par. 248(1) et par. 37(1))

Structured Process of Experimentation & Contemporaneous Documentation: Requires formulated hypotheses, systematic testing protocols, and measurable experimental results generated contemporaneously with the work.

Failed to provide any objective evidence of hypotheses, testing protocols, or measurable results for 2006 and 2009; however, maintained physical consumables records and documented test results for portions of 2007 and 2008.

Objective Contemporaneous & Physical Corroboration: Claims lacking contemporaneous test logs and hypotheses fail (2006 and 2009 denied in full); claims corroborated by physical evidence of consumables and documented test results succeed (2007 and 2008 partially allowed in 2025 TCC 173).
ITA s. 152(4)(a)(i) & s. 163(2) (L.I.R. sous-al. 152(4)a)(i) et par. 163(2))

Statute-Barred Reassessment & Gross Negligence Penalties: The CRA may reopen years beyond the normal reassessment period if the return contains a misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default, and impose 50% penalties for gross negligence.
Filed T661 technical reports containing plagiarized supplier website text and unsubstantiated experimental claims, relying on initial "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) notices as final (2025 TCC 173).

Minister's Burden Satisfied by Negligent/Plagiarized T661 Filings: Plagiarized or misleading technical descriptions in Form T661 constitute a misrepresentation attributable to neglect or carelessness under s. 152(4)(a)(i), reopening closed AAF years and justifying s. 163(2) gross negligence penalties (2025 TCC 173).
ITA s. 160 & Common Venture Liability (L.I.R. art. 160 et responsabilité pénale des administrateurs)

Personal Liability of Directors and Shareholders: Directors participating in a common venture face equal criminal fines under s. 239(1.1); shareholders receiving corporate transfers while tax debts exist face strict joint and several liability under s. 160.
Maged and Shady Elhami personally orchestrated the false 2010 claim (2017 QCCQ 2684) and extracted corporate value during years subject to retroactive SR&ED reassessment (2025 TCC 173).

Strict Derivative & Penal Liability: Co-directors in a common venture (aventure commune) bear equal penal liability per count (2017 QCCQ 2684); non-arm's-length transferees are strictly liable up to the amount received under s. 160 ITA with no due diligence defence (2025 TCC 173).

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the holdings of 2017 QCCQ 2684 and 2025 TCC 173 into a rigorous operational compliance methodology, the following two applied case studies examine realistic Canadian industrial R&D projects confronting the exact legal, contractual, accounting, and technical pitfalls that caused Tempora's penal convictions and statute-barred reassessments.
Case Study 1: Subcontracted High-Temperature Plasma Coating & Thermal Engineering in Quebec Manufacturing (Remediating the 2017 QCCQ 2684 Subcontractor, Accrual, and CRA Audit Pitfalls)
Project Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

Boréal Thermique Avancée inc. ("Boréal"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (société privée sous contrôle canadien — SPCC) headquartered in Montréal, designs high-watt-density industrial immersion heaters for corrosive petrochemical processing. During its fiscal year ending October 31, 2026, Boréal initiates an R&D project to develop a plasma-sprayed ceramic-metallic (cermet) dielectric barrier coating capable of withstanding supercritical acidic fluid temperatures above 400°C without micro-fissure delamination. Lacking an atmospheric plasma spray (APS) reactor in-house, Boréal's two engineering directors enter discussions with MétaPlasma Québec inc. ("MétaPlasma"), an arm's-length Montréal metallurgical engineering firm, to perform experimental plasma deposition trials.

As Boréal approaches its October 31 fiscal year-end, the project confronts three acute legal and accounting pitfalls directly analogous to the misconduct sanctioned in 2017 QCCQ 2684. First, although Boréal and MétaPlasma discussed a multi-phase $1,200,000 budgetary quote in June 2026, no formal contract was confirmed, and only $180,000 of preliminary Phase 1 feasibility deposition trials were actually executed prior to October 31; nevertheless, Boréal's directors contemplate requesting a backdated $1,200,000 invoice from MétaPlasma covering the entire multi-year proposal so they can deliver it to Boréal's external CPA and claim the full amount on Schedule T2SCH31 for 2026. Second, the $1,200,000 quote bundles eligible experimental plasma parameter trials together with $450,000 of commercial production tooling and capital equipment fabrication that are statutorily excluded from SR&ED under subsection 248(1) and subsection 127(9) ITA. Third, if Boréal files the inflated $1,200,000 subcontractor claim, the CRA's pre-disbursement verification unit will inevitably demand the underlying contract, proof of payment, and an on-site inspection of MétaPlasma's plasma facility—creating the exact audit crisis that led the Elhami brothers to lie to CRA officials, attempt to suborn Pyro Genesis, and incur $3,972,882 in initial criminal fines under subsection 239(1.1) ITA.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Internal Accounting Controls

To eliminate the "common venture" (aventure commune) criminal exposure under paragraphs 239(1.1)(a) and (c) ITA identified by Judge Tremblay in 2017 QCCQ 2684, Boréal must establish an institutional Three-Way Match SR&ED Governance Protocol prior to recording any R&D accrual in its General Ledger or transmitting financial documents to its external CPA. Under this governance structure, corporate accounting policy strictly prohibits booking any subcontractor expenditure based on quotes, unconfirmed proposals, or backdated invoices. Instead, an accounting entry to the SR&ED Subcontractor Expense account requires three concurrent, date-stamped artifacts: an executed bilateral Statement of Work signed prior to the commencement of testing; a Technical Milestone Completion Certificate signed by both MétaPlasma's lead metallurgist and Boréal's R&D Director certifying the exact physical experiments completed on or before October 31; and a sequential commercial invoice matching the completed milestone value ($180,000). Furthermore, rather than misleading the external accountant with unverified invoices as occurred in 2017 QCCQ 2684, Boréal's directors must furnish the external CPA with a signed SR&ED Management Representation Letter accompanied by the executed contract, milestone sign-off sheets, and wire transfer confirmations demonstrating actual payment within 180 days of fiscal year-end in compliance with subsection 127(26) ITA.
Step 2: Restructuring Subcontractor Contract Terms

To satisfy the statutory requirements of subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii) and subsection 127(9) ITA—which mandate that subcontracted SR&ED be performed in Canada "on behalf of" (pour le compte de) the claimant—Boréal and MétaPlasma must replace the informal budgetary quote with a formal, legally binding Master SR&ED Subcontracting Agreement executed before work begins. This contract must explicitly define the technical scope of work in Schedule A (Eligible Experimental SR&ED Services) by specifying the controlled experimental variables to be tested by MétaPlasma (such as varying plasma torch amperage between 500 A and 700 A, hydrogen/argon carrier gas ratios, and nano-Al₂O₃ powder feed rates), while strictly segregating all commercial tooling and capital equipment fabrication into Schedule B (Non-SR&ED Commercial Deliverables) so that zero Schedule B costs ever enter Form T661 Line 340. Crucially, the agreement must enforce milestone-based fiscal cut-offs, ensuring that only Milestone 1 ($180,000)—representing the work physically performed prior to October 31, 2026—is invoiced and claimed in the 2026 taxation year, whereas Milestones 2 and 3 remain contractually contingent and are claimed in 2027 only as actual experimental work is performed. The contract must also vest all resulting intellectual property, raw test data, and physical test coupons in Boréal, and include a mandatory CRA Audit & Site-Visit Cooperation Covenant obligating MétaPlasma to preserve technician timesheets and reactor logs and to participate transparently in any CRA on-site verification.
Step 3: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Contemporaneous Deliverables

To ensure that the $180,000 Milestone 1 claim satisfies both the technical review by the CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and the financial audit by the CRA Financial Reviewer, Boréal must require MétaPlasma to deliver a contemporaneous Technical Substantiation Package as a contractual condition precedent to payment of the $180,000 invoice. This package must contain the raw, system-generated atmospheric plasma spray (APS) reactor data logs bearing machine timestamps from the 2026 fiscal period, documenting substrate pre-heat temperatures, plasma plume enthalpy readings, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) cross-sectional porosity measurements for each experimental run. Simultaneously, Boréal must take physical custody of the coated test coupons—including delaminated and failed prototypes—and catalogue them in Boréal's Montréal laboratory with engraved serial numbers cross-referenced directly to MétaPlasma's milestone report and invoice line items.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and CRA Pre-Payout Verification Conduct

When the CRA selects Boréal's 2026 SR&ED return for pre-payout verification, Boréal executes a transparent audit-response protocol that completely avoids the obstruction and subornation pitfalls of 2017 QCCQ 2684. Prior to responding to the CRA's initial information request, Boréal's tax counsel conducts an internal pre-audit reconciliation; if any inadvertent timing or calculation error is identified prior to CRA audit contact, it is disclosed immediately through a formal voluntary adjustment rather than waiting until the morning of a site visit after a failed cover-up. During the CRA on-site inspection at Boréal's and MétaPlasma's facilities, both companies jointly present the executed Master Subcontracting Agreement, the dated reactor logs, the physical failed test coupons, and the reconciled General Ledger entries, establishing unimpeachable technical and financial integrity.

body.text: Case Study 2: Railway & Industrial Heating Element Development (Remediating the 2025 TCC 173 Plagiarized Literature, Technological Uncertainty, Consumables, and Statute-Barred Reassessment Pitfalls)
Project Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

Systèmes Ferro-Caloriques Laurentides inc. ("Laurentides"), a Quebec-based manufacturer of electric railway track-switch heaters and UV-integrated industrial air-heating units (closely paralleling the commercial profile in 2025 TCC 173 and related corporate operations), undertakes a three-year internal R&D project to develop a compact, vibration-resistant magnesium oxide (MgO) compacted tubular heating element capable of rapid thermal cycling in Arctic rail environments without dielectric breakdown.

In preparing its SR&ED claims across three consecutive taxation years, Laurentides falls into the exact evidentiary and procedural traps adjudicated by the Tax Court of Canada in 2025 TCC 173. First, Laurentides retains an external contingency-fee preparer who copies and pastes background theory on dielectric thermal conductivity, watt-density thresholds, and nickel-chromium (NiCr) resistance wire metallurgy directly from third-party raw material supplier and manufacturer websites into Boxes 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661. Second, because the CRA processes the first two taxation years on an "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) basis without an audit review, Laurentides' management assumes those years are permanently closed, neglects to archive formal hypothesis-and-test records for Year 3, and pays out substantial cash dividends to its two controlling shareholders. Third, Laurentides claims $220,000 in alloy sheathing, MgO powder, and resistance wire as SR&ED materials consumed (matériaux consommés), but commingles experimental prototype scrap with routine commercial production inventory.

Under the precedent of 2025 TCC 173, Laurentides faces severe retroactive exposure: the plagiarized supplier website text in Form T661 empowers the Minister to reopen the statute-barred AAF years under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA on the ground of negligent misrepresentation, disallow the claims for failure to prove technological uncertainty and systematic experimentation, impose 50% gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA, and assess the controlling shareholders personally for the prior dividends under section 160 ITA.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Blueprint
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance, T661 Originality Auditing, and Section 160 Shareholder Protection

To neutralize the statute-barred reassessment trigger under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA and gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA established in 2025 TCC 173, Laurentides must institute a mandatory T661 Technical Authenticity & Legal Review Protocol governing all external and internal claim preparation. Under this protocol, every draft Form T661 narrative must undergo automated plagiarism and originality screening against supplier websites, commercial catalogues, academic literature, and prior-year T661 filings before submission to the CRA, accompanied by a signed Lead Engineer Attestation confirming that every technical statement reflects original internal engineering records. Furthermore, recognizing the holding in 2025 TCC 173 that an "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) notice does not insulate a return from reassessment under subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA, Laurentides must conduct a proactive legal and technical audit of all prior AAF filings within the preceding six years to remediate any defective narratives before a CRA audit is initiated. Simultaneously, to insulate the controlling shareholders from strict derivative liability under section 160 ITA, Laurentides must replace discretionary unremunerated shareholder transfers or vulnerable dividends with documented T4 employment remuneration tied directly to the directors' hands-on R&D engineering supervision, thereby both eliminating section 160 transfer exposure and establishing an eligible direct SR&ED wage base under section 37 ITA.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation to Demarcate Supplier Literature from Technological Uncertainty

To overcome the Tax Court of Canada's objection in 2025 TCC 173 regarding supplier and manufacturer website content, Laurentides must fundamentally restructure how third-party technical literature is referenced in Form T661. Supplier and manufacturer specifications must never be copied into the technical narrative as if they represent the taxpayer's own experimental analysis. Instead, Laurentides must explicitly cite vendor data sheets in Box 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties) solely to establish the baseline boundary of publicly available standard knowledge, demonstrating precisely why standard vendor guidelines fail to solve the system-level engineering conflict. Specifically, the Box 242 narrative must state that while Supplier X's published specification sheet (Ref. #MGO-2026-04) establishes that standard fused MgO powder compacted to 3.0 g/cm³ maintains a dielectric strength of 15 kV/mm at 20°C under static conditions, publicly available metallurgical data and vendor engineering tables cannot predict grain-boundary dielectric breakdown when the element is subjected to simultaneous railway mechanical vibration and rapid thermal shock from −40°C to 600°C in under 90 seconds, because increasing swaging compaction density above 3.2 g/cm³ to improve heat transfer crushes the crystalline lattice and induces coil short-circuiting. Framing the narrative in this manner transforms supplier website data from a fatal plagiarism liability into objective proof that the taxpayer exhausted the public state of the art before commencing experimentation.
Step 3: Restructuring Procurement and Shop-Floor Tracking for Materials Consumed or Transformed

In 2025 TCC 173, the Tax Court of Canada allowed specific portions of Tempora's 2007 and 2008 projects strictly because Tempora adduced physical evidence of consumables (matériaux consommés) and documented test results. To replicate that exact evidentiary standard across all claimed years under paragraph 37(1)(a) and subsection 127(9) ITA, Laurentides must segregate all experimental materials from commercial inventory at the point of requisition. Every batch of Incoloy 800 sheathing, doped MgO powder, and resistance wire used for experimental prototypes must be issued under a dedicated SR&ED-EXP work-order series linked to a specific experimental hypothesis log. Because materials only qualify as materials consumed or transformed if they are destroyed or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED activity, Laurentides must maintain a contemporaneous Destructive Testing & Scrap Disposition Register recording the batch number, invoice reference, mass (kg), photographic evidence of cross-sectioned failed elements, and scrap recycling certificates, ensuring complete traceability and preventing any inadvertent commercial sale that would trigger SR&ED ITC recapture under subsection 127(27) ITA.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking via a Contemporaneous Scientific Ledger

To satisfy the Tax Court's requirement in 2025 TCC 173 for objective evidence of scientific methodology—and avoid the total disallowance imposed on Tempora's 2006 and 2009 claims where evidence of hypotheses, testing, and measurable results was absent—Laurentides must maintain a contemporaneous Experimental Hypothesis & Quantitative Test Ledger throughout the fiscal year, structured as follows:

cells: Doping fused MgO with nano-boron nitride (h-BN) compacted via 4-pass rotary swaging to 3.25 g/cm³ will maintain dielectric leakage current at ≤0.5 mA across 500 thermal shock cycles (−40°C to 600°C).
Fabricated 12 prototype elements (Batch #SR-01, Incoloy 800 + doped MgO, Invoice #4402). Subjected to environmental chamber thermal cycling and shaker table protocol.

Dielectric breakdown occurred at Cycle 142 (mean leakage current spiked to 4.8 mA). Post-mortem SEM cross-section (Log #SEM-88) revealed h-BN platelet agglomeration along the inner coil radius during 18% swaging reduction.

Hypothesis Refuted: Standard 18% single-pass swaging shears h-BN platelets, creating conductive micro-voids. Formulate new hypothesis (EXP-2026-02) testing stepped annealing between 9% swaging passes.
Introducing an intermediate inert-argon stress-relief anneal between two 9.5% swaging passes will prevent platelet shear and preserve lattice packing density ≥3.25 g/cm³.
Fabricated 15 prototype elements (Batch #SR-02, 38 kg MgO/h-BN powder consumed, Invoice #4519). Tested under identical 500-cycle Arctic thermal-vibration profile.
Achieved 500 cycles with mean leakage current of 0.32 mA at 600°C and thermal response time reduced by 22% (Test Report #TR-2026-09). Destructive sectioning confirmed uniform grain distribution.
Hypothesis Validated: Technological advancement achieved; experimental consumables (38 kg) logged to scrap manifest #SC-02 and cross-referenced to Form T661 Line 320.
Substituting a stepped dual-pitch 80/20 cold-pin weld geometry will eliminate localized hot-spot arcing at the terminal transition zone under harmonic rail resonance.
Fabricated 10 prototype elements (Batch #SR-03, 14 kg Incoloy 800 sheathing consumed, Invoice #4688). Subjected to infrared thermography and accelerated harmonic fatigue testing.
Infrared thermography (Log #IR-204) recorded a 65°C reduction in terminal transition temperature and zero weld micro-cracking after 1,000,000 vibration cycles.
Hypothesis Validated: Quantified knowledge gain documented for Form T661 Box 244 and Box 246; all 10 destructively sectioned units recorded in Scrap Register #SC-03.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Governance

The combined jurisprudence of the Court of Quebec in Sa Majesté la Reine c. Maged Elhami, Shady Elhami et Les éléments chauffants Tempora inc. (2017 QCCQ 2684, reviewed on appeal (Count 1 convictions upheld, Count 2 conditionally stayed, and fines varied to $1,000,000) in 2018 QCCS 2576, 2018 QCCA 1488, and SCC Docket 38388) and the Tax Court of Canada in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173) establishes a comprehensive enforcement doctrine for Canadian corporate taxpayers, R&D directors, external accountants, and technical tax advisors. In the criminal sphere, 2017 QCCQ 2684 confirms that submitting unconfirmed or backdated third-party subcontractor invoices, deceiving external accountants into recording false R&D accruals in financial statements, and attempting to mislead or suborn third parties during a CRA pre-payment verification audit will trigger mandatory statutory fines of 50% to 200% on the full credit claimed under paragraph 239(1.1)(g) ITA, even where the CRA intercepts the claim before a single dollar is disbursed and even where the taxpayer files an eleventh-hour amendment on the morning of a site visit. In the civil sphere, 2025 TCC 173 proves that "Accepted as Filed" (AAF) processing offers zero permanent finality when Form T661 technical narratives contain plagiarized supplier website text or negligent misrepresentations: the CRA can invoke subparagraph 152(4)(a)(i) ITA a decade later to reopen statute-barred years, disallow unsubstantiated claims, impose 50% gross negligence penalties under subsection 163(2) ITA, and pursue shareholders personally under section 160 ITA, leaving only those project segments supported by authentic, contemporaneous test logs and physical evidence of consumed materials standing at trial.
